canon.title: The Scientific Revolution, 1543–1727
canon.about: Classical facts of the Scientific Revolution, from De revolutionibus and the death of Copernicus to the death of Newton: science foremost, with its philosophy, its patrons and its politics; the great correspondences (Mersenne's, Oldenburg's), the trials of Galileo, the founding of the Royal Society and the Académie, and the quarrels over priority. Dates are written as their sources write them: England in Old Style (julian-march, the legal year from 25 March) until 1752, the Catholic continent in the Gregorian calendar from 1582, Protestant Germany and Denmark in the Julian until 1700. Its selection is that of the standard biographies: famous men of print and letters, almost all in western Europe; artisans, instrument makers, assistants, women other than a queen, and science outside Europe are absent, and the record is densest where the letters survive. A seed canon, drafted from general knowledge by a language model, each assertion naming the standard reference it is to be checked against; none is checked yet.

beings.name: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
beings.note: Copernicus's book, carried from its printing to its suspension by the Index.

beings.name: Cosimo II de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany
Federico Cesi
beings.note: Founder of the Accademia dei Lincei (1603), which he stands for here.

beings.name: Urban VIII (Maffeo Barberini)
beings.note: Cardinal Maffeo Barberini until his election as pope on 6 August 1623.

beings.name: Pierre de Fermat
beings.note: Born 1601 by the older reckoning (Mahoney); a birth in 1607 has since been argued.

beings.name: Isaac Newton
beings.note: Born 25 December 1642 Old Style (4 January 1643 New Style); died 20 March 1726/7 Old Style (31 March 1727 New Style).

occasions.label: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium printed by Petreius, from the manuscript Rheticus brought from Frombork
occasions.note: Rheticus saw the first part through the press in 1542 and left for Leipzig; Osiander added the unsigned preface. The book was finished in the spring of 1543.

occasions.label: Death of Copernicus
occasions.note: That the printed book reached him on the day he died is a story first told by Tiedemann Giese.

occasions.label: Galileo thanks Kepler for the Mysterium cosmographicum and confesses himself a Copernican in private
Kepler arrives at Tycho's castle of Benátky
Kepler quarrels with Tycho over the terms of his employment, leaves in anger, and then apologises in writing
Tycho presents Kepler to the emperor, and the Rudolphine Tables are proposed in Rudolf's name
occasions.note: The month of the audience is not established; Tycho had been the emperor's mathematician since 1599.

occasions.label: Death of Tycho Brahe; Kepler records his last words, Ne frustra vixisse videar
Kepler appointed imperial mathematician in Tycho's place
Kepler's Astronomia nova, the first two laws, dedicated to Rudolf II
Sidereus nuncius, with the satellites of Jupiter named the Medicean stars for Cosimo II
Kepler's Dissertatio cum Nuncio sidereo, an open letter of support to Galileo
Galileo named Chief Mathematician and Philosopher to the Grand Duke
Galileo celebrated in Rome and enrolled in Cesi's Accademia dei Lincei
The dispute on floating bodies at the Grand Duke's table, where Cardinal Barberini takes Galileo's side
Death of Rudolf II
Galileo's Letters on Sunspots published by the Lincei
Bellarmine admonishes Galileo to abandon the Copernican opinion
occasions.note: Whether a stricter injunction, not to hold, teach or defend it in any way, was also served that day is disputed; the minute that says so was decisive in 1633.

occasions.label: The Congregation of the Index suspends De revolutionibus until it is corrected
occasions.note: The decree is certain; Bellarmine's part in the congregation's deliberation is to be checked.

occasions.label: Bellarmine gives Galileo a certificate that he has neither abjured nor been penanced
Death of Cosimo II
Il Saggiatore, published by the Lincei and dedicated to the new pope, Urban VIII
Galileo, after a stay with Cesi, has six audiences with Urban VIII, who allows a hypothetical treatment of the two systems
Descartes to Mersenne: the eternal truths are created by God
Death of Federico Cesi
The Dialogue on the Two Chief World Systems, with the pope's favourite argument in the mouth of Simplicio
Galileo before the Holy Office: interrogated from 12 April, sentenced and made to abjure on 22 June
occasions.note: Urban presided over the congregation of 16 June that decided the sentence; he was not at the abjuration.

occasions.label: Descartes tells Mersenne that, hearing of Galileo's condemnation, he will not publish Le Monde
The Discours de la méthode, with the Dioptrique, the Météores and the Géométrie; Mersenne handles it in Paris
Fermat's objections to the Dioptrique reach Descartes through Mersenne
occasions.note: Fermat had seen the Dioptrique in proof through Beaugrand; the months of the exchange are to be checked.

occasions.label: The dispute over Fermat's method of maxima and minima and of tangents, through Mersenne
Descartes writes to Fermat in conciliation, acknowledging his method
occasions.note: In letters to others Descartes went on disparaging Fermat.

occasions.label: Descartes to Mersenne on Galileo's Two New Sciences: he builds without foundations
The young Pascal's Essai pour les coniques; Descartes, sent it by Mersenne, judges that he learnt it from Desargues
The Meditationes with the Objections Mersenne collected, Hobbes's the third, and Descartes's dismissive Replies
Death of Galileo
Descartes visits Pascal; they disagree about the vacuum
occasions.note: Jacqueline Pascal's letter to her sister describes the two visits.

occasions.label: Death of Mersenne
Descartes arrives at the court of Queen Christina
occasions.note: Sweden kept the Julian calendar; the date is given New Style, as Descartes and his biographers give it.

occasions.label: Death of Descartes
occasions.note: 1 February 1650 in Sweden's Julian calendar.

occasions.label: The correspondence of Pascal and Fermat on the division of stakes
Wallis's Elenchus geometriae Hobbianae refutes Hobbes's squaring of the circle in De corpore
Hobbes's Six Lessons to the Professors of the Mathematiques, against Wallis
Hooke, Boyle's assistant, builds the air pump
After Wren's lecture at Gresham College, twelve men, Boyle among them, found a college for experimental learning
Hobbes's Dialogus physicus de natura aeris attacks Boyle's air pump and the new society
Oldenburg visits Spinoza and their correspondence begins
Spinoza's criticism of Boyle's experiments on nitre, sent through Oldenburg
occasions.note: The letter (Ep. 6) is undated; winter or spring 1662.

occasions.label: The first royal charter: the Royal Society, under the king's patronage, with Oldenburg one of its two secretaries
occasions.note: Oldenburg and Wilkins are named secretaries in the charters of 1662 and 1663; which first named them is to be checked.

occasions.label: Death of Pascal
Hooke, released from Boyle's service, made the Society's Curator of Experiments
Oldenburg sends Spinoza Boyle's answer on nitre
Hooke's Micrographia, printed with the Society's imprimatur
occasions.note: January 1664/5: January 1665 by the historical year, when Pepys bought his copy.

occasions.label: The first number of the Philosophical Transactions, Oldenburg's own venture
occasions.note: 6 March 1664/5: 1665 by the historical year.

occasions.label: The Académie royale des sciences first meets in the King's Library, Huygens its leading member
Barrow sends Newton's De analysi to Collins
Newton's letter on light and colours read to the Society
occasions.note: 8 February 1671/2; Newton had been elected a Fellow on 11 January 1671/2 after showing his reflecting telescope.

occasions.label: Hooke's critique of Newton's theory read to the Society and sent on by Oldenburg
Leibniz, newly in Paris, begins to learn mathematics under Huygens
Huygens's objections to Newton's theory of colours, sent through Oldenburg
Leibniz shows his calculating machine to the Royal Society; Hooke finds fault with it
occasions.note: Leibniz dated his letters New Style; the Society's minutes give the meeting Old Style.

occasions.label: After the objections to his theory, Newton asks Oldenburg to remove him from the Society
occasions.note: 8 March 1672/3. Oldenburg talked him round and the dues were waived.

occasions.label: Leibniz elected a Fellow of the Royal Society
Leibniz demonstrates his calculating machine before the Académie
Charles II's warrant makes Flamsteed his astronomical observator
Hooke's conciliatory letter and Newton's reply: if I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants
occasions.note: 20 January and 5 February 1675/6: 1676 by the historical year. Some read Newton's phrase as a gibe at Hooke's stature.

occasions.label: Newton's Epistola prior, for Leibniz, sent through Oldenburg: the binomial series
Leibniz, in London again, reads Newton's De analysi among Collins's papers and takes notes
occasions.note: The notes were turned against him in 1712.

occasions.label: Leibniz visits Spinoza and talks with him for days
Newton's Epistola posterior, through Oldenburg, hiding the method of fluxions in an anagram
occasions.note: 24 October 1676 Old Style is 3 November New Style; Leibniz received it only in 1677.

occasions.label: Death of Spinoza
Leibniz answers through Oldenburg, setting out his differential calculus
occasions.note: Dated New Style by Leibniz, though Hanover kept the Julian calendar until 1700. Newton did not reply.

occasions.label: Death of Oldenburg
Hooke, now secretary, reopens correspondence with Newton: the composition of orbital motion and the inverse square
occasions.note: 24 November 1679 to 17 January 1679/80. Hooke read Newton's mistaken spiral to the Society, and Newton broke off.

occasions.label: Death of Hobbes
Death of John Collins
Halley asks Newton what orbit an inverse-square force would give; an ellipse, Newton says, for he has calculated it
Death of Charles II
occasions.note: 6 February 1684/5.

occasions.label: Book I of the Principia before the Society; Hooke claims the inverse square, Halley reports it, Newton rages and strikes Hooke out
The Principia published at Halley's expense, with a scholium acknowledging Leibniz's method
occasions.note: The scholium to Book II, Lemma 2 was cut from the third edition of 1726.

occasions.label: Huygens in London meets Newton at the Royal Society and goes with him to recommend him to the king
Death of Boyle
Newton visits Flamsteed for lunar observations
Death of Huygens
The quarrel over the lunar observations: Newton wants Flamsteed's observations and not his calculations
Newton solves Johann Bernoulli's brachistochrone challenge in a night and answers anonymously
occasions.note: 29 January 1696/7, as Catherine Conduitt told it.

occasions.label: The solutions in the Acta Eruditorum; Bernoulli knows the anonymous English one, tanquam ex ungue leonem
occasions.note: Saxony kept the Julian calendar until 1700.

occasions.label: The reformed Académie elects its first foreign associates, Newton, Leibniz and the Bernoullis among them
Death of Hooke
Newton elected President of the Royal Society
Keill's paper in the Philosophical Transactions charges Leibniz with taking the calculus from Newton
occasions.note: Written in 1708, printed in 1710.

occasions.label: Leibniz complains to the Society's secretary of Keill and asks for a retraction
The Society, under its president Newton, appoints a committee on the dispute
The committee's report, drafted by Newton himself, finds for Newton and Keill; printed as the Commercium epistolicum
occasions.note: Newton's authorship was secret; the codebook counts a secret act where it is done (§6).

occasions.label: Halley, under Newton's direction, prints Flamsteed's observations as the Historia coelestis, against Flamsteed's will
Leibniz's anonymous Charta volans, citing the judgement of a leading mathematician, Johann Bernoulli
Newton's anonymous Account of the Commercium epistolicum in the Philosophical Transactions
occasions.note: January and February 1714/15.

occasions.label: Death of Leibniz
Flamsteed obtains the unsold copies of Halley's edition and burns them
Death of Flamsteed
Death of Newton
occasions.note: 20 March 1726/7 Old Style: 31 March 1727 New Style.

ties.note: At his death Tycho asks Kepler to build the tables on the Tychonic system, and leaves him the observations in effect.
The salary was always in arrears.
Galileo would not declare himself publicly in 1597, and left Kepler's request for a telescope unanswered in 1610.
Not a rivalry in natural knowledge but a controversy over it: the cardinal's admonition, then his protective certificate.
Barberini praised Galileo in his poem Adulatio perniciosa (1620); the pope took Simplicio's argument for a mockery of his own.
The Lincei courted the Barberini; the pope's nephew Francesco was made a Lincean.
The reconciliation of 1638 is the act remembered; Descartes's private disparagement went on (codebook §6, mixed acts).
They never met; Descartes judged Galileo's science at a distance, through Mersenne.
The young Pascal came with his father to Mersenne's academy.
Descartes to Huygens after the visit of 1647: Pascal has too much vacuum in his head.
Descartes refused to go on corresponding with Hobbes in 1641.
He taught her at five in the morning that winter.
Hobbes was never elected.
A Fellow since his London visit of 1663.
A courteous controversy at a distance, through Oldenburg; neither gave way.
Huygens left Paris for good in 1681 and was not recalled after Colbert's death.
Their correspondence of the 1690s disagreed about the calculus and the cause of gravity without a break; no rupture is recorded, so the tie keeps its sign.
He had hoped in vain for a paid place in 1675-76.
Hooke criticised the machine before the Society and promised a better one.
In 1711 he appealed to the Society as a Fellow; its committee, packed by Newton, judged against him.

Cordial through Oldenburg in 1676-77, though Newton hid his method in an anagram; the open quarrel follows Fatio's insinuation (1699) and Keill's charge (1708). Newton carried it on after Leibniz's death.

The exchange of 1679-80 is coded by what it is remembered for, Hooke's suggestion of the inverse square; Newton resented its sequel (codebook §6, mixed acts). Newton published the Opticks only after Hooke's death.
In 1675-76 Hooke accused Oldenburg of betraying his spring watch to Huygens; that quarrel is not coded here.
Halley had discussed the inverse square with Hooke and Wren in January 1683/4, and mediated in 1686.
Bernoulli later denied that the judgement in the Charta volans was his.
Leibniz later played the meeting down.
